stem.text: Which substance does not give HCl(g) when water is added to it?

explanation.text: Across Period 3 the chlorides change from ionic (NaCl, MgCl<sub>2</sub>) to covalent (Al<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>6</sub>, SiCl<sub>4</sub>, PCl<sub>5</sub>). Ionic chlorides simply dissolve; covalent chlorides are hydrolysed by water, releasing white fumes of HCl.

MgCl<sub>2</sub> dissolves to give Mg<sup>2+</sup>(aq) and Cl<sup>–</sup>(aq); the solution is only slightly acidic (pH about 6.5) because the hydrated Mg<sup>2+</sup> ion is weakly acidic, but no HCl gas is given off. SiCl<sub>4</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → SiO<sub>2</sub> + 4HCl and PCl<sub>5</sub> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O → H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> + 5HCl. Al<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>6</sub> reacts vigorously with a little water to give fumes of HCl.

optionAnalysis.text: Correct. Magnesium chloride is ionic and dissolves to give hydrated ions; the solution is slightly acidic but no HCl(g) is released.
Covalent aluminium chloride is hydrolysed by water and gives off fumes of HCl.
Silicon tetrachloride is hydrolysed completely: SiCl<sub>4</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → SiO<sub>2</sub> + 4HCl.
Phosphorus(V) chloride is hydrolysed: PCl<sub>5</sub> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O → H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> + 5HCl.

reasoningChain: Classify the chlorides: MgCl<sub>2</sub> ionic; Al<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>6</sub>, SiCl<sub>4</sub>, PCl<sub>5</sub> covalent.
Covalent chlorides are hydrolysed by water and release HCl.
The ionic chloride only dissolves, so MgCl<sub>2</sub> is the one that does not give HCl(g).

inferredMistakes.text: Linking the slightly acidic pH of MgCl<sub>2</sub>(aq) with HCl being released and so ruling out A.
Overlooking the word not and choosing a chloride that does give HCl.
